advances: One full-dimensional compact ordinary convex body and a prescribed interior mark. The least upper comparison constant is dimensionwise d+1; it is approached at an interior mark moving toward a vertex of a fixed simplex and is never attained. No base-energy conversion, sampled-mixture claim, or mixed halfspace guarantee follows.

proof:
**Retained cap.** Translate $y$ to $0$. Apply the one-packet case of accepted fact 2c093df4eb8158a9 to a mass $t>0$ at the origin. For its affine tests with $\ell(0)\le0$, the inequalities are automatic. Those with $\ell(0)>0$ normalize to $\ell(x)=1+u\cdot x$. Hence the feasible masses are precisely the positive $t$ bounded by $\inf_u G(u)$, where $G(u)=\int_K(1+u\cdot x)_+\,dx$. The inner ball centered at $0$ gives $G(u)\ge\int_{rB}(u\cdot x)_+\,dx=c\|u\|$ for $rB\subset K$ and $c>0$, so the continuous convex function $G$ attains its minimum. At nonzero $u$ the zero affine level is Lebesgue null, and near $u=0$ the affine function is positive throughout $K$. Bounded difference quotients justify differentiation under the integral, giving $\nabla G(u)=\int_{K\cap\{1+u\cdot x\ge0\}}x\,dx$. At any minimizer $u_*$, the cap $D=K\cap\{1+u_*\cdot x\ge0\}$ contains an inner ball at $0$ and has zero first moment. Thus $G(u_*)=|D|=T_K(0)>0$. Equality in $\int_K(1+u_*\cdot x)f\,dx\le G(u_*)$ for a maximizing density forces $f=\mathbf1_D$ almost everywhere, since the hinge level is null (or empty when $u_*=0$). The cap is unique as a body because full-dimensional compact convex bodies that differ as sets differ in volume on their symmetric difference. Every convex subbody with the required centroid is feasible by its indicator. If $0$ is the centroid of $K$, then $f=1$ is optimal. Otherwise $D$ must be proper, and its cutting plane meets the interior of $K$: the positive side contains an inner ball and the complement has positive volume. Two distinct normalized proper cut parameters cannot agree on the positive region in the interior, so $u_*$ is unique off the centroid.

**Lower comparison.** Accepted fact d90ba05577427854 applies to this full-dimensional compact body and interior mark, giving a unique attained energy optimizer $a_*$. For $L>0$, strict convexity gives $L^{-d-1}\ge (1-(d+1)(L-1))_+$, with equality only at $L=1$. At $L(x)=1+a_*\cdot x$ this yields $E_K(0)\ge G(-(d+1)a_*)\ge T_K(0)$. If $a_*\ne0$, then $L=1$ only on a Lebesgue-null plane, so the first inequality is strict. The zero parameter is optimal exactly at the centroid, by the gradient at zero and strict convexity in d90ba05577427854. In that case $E_K(0)=T_K(0)=|K|$.

**Upper comparison for $d\ge2$.** The centroid case already gives the strict upper bound, so take the proper cap above. Write $T=T_K(0)$, $B=d+1$, and $s=1+u_*\cdot x$. The pushforward of Lebesgue measure on $K$ by this height has density $\phi(s)=\mathcal H^{d-1}(K\cap\{1+u_*\cdot x=s\})/\|u_*\|$ by linear coarea, with finite support interval $[a,b]$ and $a<0<b$. Extend $\phi$ by zero off that interval. Convex inclusion of interpolated parallel sections and Brunn–Minkowski in dimension $d-1$ give concavity of $\phi^{1/(d-1)}$ on $(a,b)$. The mass and centroid of $D$ give $\int_0^b\phi(s)\,ds=\int_0^b s\phi(s)\,ds=T$.

Fix a point of $D$ at height $b$. Its homothety of $D$ with ratio $1-t/b$ lies in $D\cap\{s\ge t\}$ for $0\le t\le b$, and has volume $(1-t/b)^d T$. Integrating this survival bound gives mean height at least $b/(d+1)$. The mean is one, so $b\le B$. Define the comparison density $\psi(s)=(dT/B^d)(B-s)^{d-1}$ for $s\le B$ and zero for $s>B$. Its mass and first moment on $[0,B]$ are both $T$, by direct integration and $B=d+1$.

The root difference $\phi^{1/(d-1)}-\psi^{1/(d-1)}$ is concave on $(a,b)$. Thus the positive set of $\phi-\psi$ in $(0,B)$ is an interval up to endpoints, since the difference is nonpositive beyond $b$. If the densities differ on a set of positive measure in $[0,B]$, then matching masses forces a nonempty positive interval. Its endpoints $r_1,r_2$ satisfy $0<r_1<r_2<B$: if $r_1=0$, the product $(s-r_2)(\phi-\psi)$ is nonpositive almost everywhere and strictly negative on a set of positive measure, contradicting the two matched moments. If $r_2=B$, use $(s-r_1)(\phi-\psi)$ with the opposite sign. Consequently the root difference at $0$ is nonpositive by continuity in the open actual support. Concavity between any $s\in(a,0)$ and an interior height in the positive interval then forces the root difference to be negative at $s$. In the alternative case where the densities agree almost everywhere on $[0,B]$, positivity of $\psi$ on $(0,B)$ forces $b=B$, and the root difference is zero on $(0,B)$ by continuity. Concavity at $0$, using any positive interior height, still forces it to be nonpositive at every $s\in(a,0)$. In both cases $\phi\le\psi$ almost everywhere below $0$. No continuity at $b$ is needed.

For any finite convex $w$ on $[0,B]$, in the unequal case subtract its affine secant at $r_1,r_2$. The result is nonpositive between them and nonnegative outside. Its product with $\phi-\psi$ is nonpositive almost everywhere, and the secant integrates to zero against $\phi-\psi$ by the two matched moments. Thus $\int_0^B w\phi\le\int_0^B w\psi$, also true when the densities agree. Take $w(s)=(B+1-s)^{-d-1}$ for $s\le B$. The test parameter $-u_*/B$ has denominator $(B+1-s)/B\ge1/B$ on all of $K$. The comparison on $[0,B]$, together with $\phi\le\psi$ below zero, gives a strict inequality on integration against $w$ over the full height range because $\phi=0$ and $\psi>0$ on $(-\infty,a)$. Finally,
$$
\int_{-\infty}^B w(s)\psi(s)\,ds
=\frac{dT}{B^d}\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{d-1}}{(1+t)^{d+1}}\,dt
=\frac{T}{B^d},
$$
using $t/(1+t)$ as the new variable. Evaluating the objective at $-u_*/B$ therefore gives $E_K(0)<B^{d+1}T/B^d=(d+1)T$.

**Simplex calculation, intervals, and sharpness.** For any simplex with vertices $v_i$ and interior barycentric mark $y$, write $w_i=v_i-y$. Positive affine denominators on $K$ correspond exactly to positive vertex values $L_i$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i L_i=1$. The projective volume identity in d90ba05577427854 gives the volume of the image simplex with vertices $w_i/L_i$: a convex combination with original weights $\mu_i$ maps to the combination with weights $\mu_i L_i/\sum_j\mu_j L_j$, and every weight vector is obtained by the inverse rescaling. Its volume is $V/\prod_i L_i$. Indeed multiplying column $i$ of the augmented vertex matrix $(w_i/L_i,1)$ by $L_i$ and subtracting the appropriate linear combination of the first $d$ rows from the last changes the last row from $L_i$ to $1$. By arithmetic–geometric mean, $\prod_i(\lambda_i L_i)\le(d+1)^{-d-1}$ with equality at $\lambda_i L_i=1/(d+1)$ for all $i$. This gives the stated simplex energy and a positive admissible optimizer.

For $d=1$, the greatest centroidal subinterval of $[-\ell,r]$ has length $2\min(\ell,r)$, so the retained-cap result gives that $T$. The simplex formula with two endpoints gives $E=4\ell r/(\ell+r)$; hence $E/T=2\max(\ell,r)/(\ell+r)<2$.

In the standard simplex, the positive region of the normalized hinge $(d+1)-\sum_i x_i/\varepsilon$ is, up to its boundary, $(d+1)\varepsilon K$. The hinge equals one at $y$ and its cap has centroid $y$. Its zero centered moment makes its indicator optimal by the inequality in the first part, including when it is the full body. Thus $T=V(d+1)^d\varepsilon^d$, and the simplex energy with barycentric coordinates $1-d\varepsilon,\varepsilon,\ldots,\varepsilon$ gives the exact ratio. Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves sharpness for each $d\ge1$; strictness at every admissible pair proves nonattainment.
statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a compact convex body with nonempty interior, and let $y\in\operatorname{int}K$. Define
$$
E_K(y)=\min_{\substack{a\in\mathbb R^d\\1+a\cdot(x-y)>0\ (x\in K)}}
\int_K[1+a\cdot(x-y)]^{-d-1}\,dx,\qquad
T_K(y)=\max_{\substack{0\le f\le1\\\int_K(x-y)f(x)\,dx=0}}\int_Kf(x)\,dx,
$$
where $f$ is Lebesgue measurable. Both extrema are attained, and the energy minimizer is unique. The maximizing density for $T_K(y)$ is the indicator, up to null sets, of a unique convex cap of centroid $y$. The cap is all of $K$ at its centroid. In particular $T_K(y)$ is the greatest volume of a convex subbody of $K$ with centroid $y$.

For every such $(K,y)$,
$$
0<T_K(y)\le E_K(y)<(d+1)T_K(y).
$$
Equality $T_K(y)=E_K(y)$ holds exactly when $y$ is the centroid of $K$. For each fixed $d\ge1$, the supremum of $E_K(y)/T_K(y)$ over these pairs is $d+1$, and no pair attains it. More precisely, if $K=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$ and $y=(\varepsilon,\ldots,\varepsilon)$ with $0<\varepsilon\le1/(d+1)$, then
$$
\frac{E_K(y)}{T_K(y)}=(d+1)(1-d\varepsilon).
$$
For an arbitrary simplex of volume $V$ and an interior mark with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, $E_K(y)=V(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. In dimension one, for $K-y=[-\ell,r]$ with $\ell,r>0$, $T_K(y)=2\min(\ell,r)$ and $E_K(y)=4\ell r/(\ell+r)$.
title: Sharp projective energy comparison with maximal centroidal retained volume
